danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Familien Rostov blev i Moskva til den 1. september, det vil sige til aftenen før fjendens indtog i byen.

Efter at Petja (den yngste Rostov-søn) var tiltrådt Obólenski-regimentet af kosakker og rejst til Bélaja Tsérkov, hvor regimentet blev oprettet, blev grevinden grebet af rædsel. Tanken om, at begge hendes sønner var i krigen, at begge var fløjet fra hendes beskyttende vinger, og at den ene eller begge i dag eller i morgen kunne blive dræbt, ligesom de tre sønner af en af hendes bekendte, ramte hende den sommer for første gang med grusom klarhed. Hun forsøgte at få Nikolaj hjem og ville selv rejse hen til Petja eller skaffe ham en stilling et sted i Petersborg, men ingen af delene viste sig mulige. Petja kunne ikke vende tilbage, medmindre hans regiment gjorde det, eller han blev overført til et andet regiment i aktiv tjeneste. Nikolaj var et sted med hæren og havde ikke sendt et ord siden sit sidste brev, hvori han udførligt havde berettet om sit møde med fyrstinde Marja. Grevinden sov ikke om natten, eller når hun faldt i søvn, drømte hun, at hun så sine sønner ligge døde. Efter mange rådslagninger og samtaler fandt greven endelig på et middel til at berolige hende. Han fik Petja overført fra Obólenski-regimentet til Bezukhovs, der lå i garnison nær Moskva. Skønt Petja ville forblive i tjenesten, ville denne overførsel give grevinden den trøst at have i det mindste én af sine sønner under sine vinger, og hun håbede at kunne arrangere det for sin Petja, så hun aldrig behøvede at slippe ham af sted igen, men altid kunne få ham anbragt steder, hvor han umuligt kunne deltage i kamp. Så længe kun Nikolaj var i fare, indbildte grevinden sig, at hun elskede sin førstefødte mere end alle sine andre børn, og bebrejdede sig endda det; men da den yngste — den uartige knægt, der var dårlig til sine lektier, altid gik og ødelagde ting i huset og var til besvær for alle, den stumpnæsede Petja med hans muntre sorte øjne og friske rosenkinder, hvor blødt dun lige var begyndt at vise sig — da han blev kastet ind blandt de store, forfærdelige, grusomme mænd, der sloges et eller andet sted om et eller andet og tilsyneladende fandt fornøjelse i det — da følte hans mor, at hun elskede ham mere, langt mere end alle sine andre børn. Jo nærmere tiden for Petjas tilbagekomst rykkede, jo mere urolig blev grevinden. Hun begyndte at tro, at hun aldrig ville opleve at se en sådan lykke. Sonjas nærværelse, hendes elskede Natasjas og endda hendes mands irriterede hende. »Hvad skal jeg med dem? Jeg vil ikke have andre end Petja,« tænkte hun.

I slutningen af august modtog familien Rostov endnu et brev fra Nikolaj. Han skrev fra Voronézj-provinsen, hvor han var sendt hen for at skaffe remonter, men brevet beroligede ikke grevinden. Nu da hun vidste, at den ene søn var uden for fare, blev hun desto mere ængstelig for Petja.

Skønt næsten alle Rostov-familiens bekendte allerede havde forladt Moskva omkring den 20. august, og skønt alle forsøgte at overtale grevinden til at komme af sted så hurtigt som muligt, ville hun ikke høre tale om at rejse, før hendes skat, hendes tilbedte Petja, var vendt tilbage. Den 28. august ankom han. Den lidenskabelige ømhed, hans mor tog imod ham med, behagede ikke den seksten-årige officer. Skønt hun skjulte sin hensigt om at holde ham under sine vinger for ham, gennemskuede Petja hendes planer, og da han instinktivt frygtede, at han ville give efter for sine følelser i hendes nærværelse — blive »kvindagtig,« som han selv udtrykte det — behandlede han hende koldt, undgik hende og holdt sig under sit ophold i Moskva udelukkende til Natasja, som han altid havde haft en særlig broderlig ømhed for, næsten som en forelskelse.

På grund af grevens sædvanlige skødesløshed var intet klar til afrejsen den 28. august, og vognene, der skulle komme fra deres godser i Rjazán og Moskva for at fjerne deres ejendele, ankom først den 30.

Fra den 28. til den 31. var hele Moskva i en oprørt tilstand af uro og bevægelse. Hver dag blev tusinder af mænd, der var såret ved Borodino, bragt ind gennem Dorogomílov-porten og ført til forskellige dele af Moskva, og tusinder af vogne bragte indbyggerne og deres ejendele ud gennem de andre porte. Trods Rostoptjins opslag, eller på grund af dem, eller uafhængigt af dem, florerede de underligste og mest modstridende rygter i byen. Nogle sagde, at ingen måtte forlade byen, andre sagde tværtimod, at alle helgenbilleder var blevet fjernet fra kirkerne, og at alle ville blive beordret til at forlade byen. Nogle sagde, at der havde været endnu et slag efter Borodino, hvori franskmændene var blevet slået, mens andre tværtimod fortalte, at den russiske hær var blevet tilintetgjort. Nogle talte om Moskva-militsen, der anført af gejstligheden ville drage til De Tre Høje; andre hviskede, at Augustin havde fået forbud mod at rejse, at forrædere var arresteret, at bønderne var i oprør og plyndrede folk på vej fra Moskva, og så videre. Men alt dette var kun snak; i virkeligheden (skønt rådet i Fili, hvor det blev besluttet at opgive Moskva, endnu ikke var afholdt) følte både de, der rejste, og de, der blev tilbage, skønt de ikke viste det, at Moskva med sikkerhed ville blive opgivet, og at de burde komme af sted så hurtigt som muligt og redde deres ejendele. Man følte, at alting pludselig ville bryde sammen og forandre sig, men indtil den 1. september var intet sket. Som en forbryder, der føres til henrettelse, ved, at han straks skal dø, men alligevel ser sig omkring og retter på huen, der sidder skævt på hovedet, fortsatte Moskva ufrivilligt sit vante liv, skønt byen vidste, at tiden for dens ødelæggelse var nær, da de livsvilkår, dens folk var vant til at underkaste sig, fuldstændig ville blive kastet om.

I de tre dage forud for besættelsen af Moskva var hele Rostov-familien optaget af forskellige gøremål. Familiens overhoved, grev Ilja Rostov, kørte ustandseligt rundt i byen og samlede de aktuelle rygter op fra alle sider og gav overfladiske og hastede ordrer derhjemme om forberedelserne til afrejsen.

Grevinden overvågede indpakningen, var utilfreds med alt, jagtede ustandseligt Petja, der altid løb fra hende, og var skinsyg på Natasja, som han tilbragte al sin tid med. Alene Sonja ledede den praktiske side af tingene ved at sørge for, at alt blev pakket ned. Men i den senere tid havde Sonja været særlig trist og tavs. Nikolajs brev, hvori han nævnte fyrstinde Marja, havde i hendes påhør fremkaldt glade kommentarer fra grevinden, der så et indgreb af Forsynet i dette møde mellem fyrstinden og Nikolaj.

»Jeg var aldrig glad for Bolkonskijs forlovelse med Natasja,« sagde grevinden, »men jeg har altid ønsket, at Nikolaj skulle gifte sig med fyrstinden, og jeg havde en anelse om, at det ville ske. Hvor ville det være dejligt!«

Sonja følte, at det var sandt: at den eneste mulighed for at redde Rostov-familiens økonomi var, at Nikolaj giftede sig med en rig kvinde, og at fyrstinden var et godt parti. Det var meget bittert for hende. Men trods sin sorg, eller måske netop på grund af den, påtog hun sig alt det vanskelige arbejde med at lede opbevaringen og indpakningen af deres ting og var travlt optaget hele dage. Greven og grevinden henvendte sig til hende, når de havde ordrer at give. Petja og Natasja derimod var langt fra at hjælpe deres forældre — de var som regel til besvær og i vejen for alle. Næsten hele dagen igennem genlød huset af deres løbende fødder, deres råb og deres spontane latter. De lo og var glade, ikke fordi der var nogen grund til at le, men fordi glæde og munterhed var i deres hjerter, og alt, hvad der skete, var derfor en anledning til glæde og latter for dem. Petja var i højt humør, fordi han havde forladt hjemmet som dreng og var vendt tilbage (som alle fortalte ham) som en fin ung mand, fordi han var hjemme, fordi han havde forladt Bélaja Tsérkov, hvor der ikke var noget håb om snart at komme i kamp, og var kommet til Moskva, hvor der ville blive kæmpet om nogle dage, og frem for alt fordi Natasja, hvis eksempel han altid fulgte, var i højt humør. Natasja var glad, fordi hun havde været trist for længe, og nu mindede intet hende om årsagen til hendes tristhed, og fordi hun følte sig godt tilpas. Hun var også lykkelig, fordi hun havde nogen til at tilbede sig: andres tilbedelse var den smørelse, hendes maskines hjul behøvede for at køre frit — og Petja tilbad hende. Frem for alt var de glade, fordi der var krig nær Moskva, der ville blive kamp ved byens porte, der blev uddelt våben, alle flygtede — rejste et eller andet sted hen, og i det hele taget skete der noget ekstraordinært, og det er altid spændende, især for de unge.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: The Rostovs remained in Moscow until September 1 — the eve of the enemy's entry into the city.

After Petya had joined Obolensky's Cossack regiment and left for Belaya Tserkov where the regiment was forming, the countess was seized with terror. The thought that both her sons were at war — that both had left the safety of her wing, and that today or tomorrow either or both might be killed, as the three sons of one of her acquaintances had been — struck her that summer for the first time with cruel clarity. She tried to get Nicholas sent home and wanted to go herself to fetch Petya, or to get him assigned somewhere in Petersburg, but neither proved possible. Petya couldn't return unless his regiment did, or unless he was transferred to another active unit. Nicholas was somewhere with the army and hadn't written since his last letter, which gave a detailed account of his meeting with Princess Mary. The countess couldn't sleep at night, and when she did she dreamed of her sons lying dead. After many consultations, the count devised a way to calm her: he got Petya transferred from Obolensky's regiment to Bezukhov's, which was training near Moscow. Though Petya would remain in service, this transfer gave the countess the consolation of having at least one son within reach, and she hoped to arrange things so he'd never be sent to battle again. As long as only Nicholas was in danger, the countess imagined she loved her firstborn more than all her other children and even reproached herself for it; but when her youngest — the scapegrace who'd been bad at lessons, always breaking things and annoying everyone, that snub-nosed Petya with his cheerful black eyes and fresh rosy cheeks where soft fuzz was just beginning to show — when he was thrown among those big, terrible, cruel men who were fighting somewhere about something and apparently enjoying it, then his mother felt she loved him more, much more, than all the rest. The nearer the time came for Petya to return, the more anxious the countess grew. She began to think she would never live to see such happiness. The presence of Sonya, of beloved Natasha, or even of her husband irritated her. "What do I need them for? I need no one but Petya," she thought.

At the end of August the Rostovs received another letter from Nicholas. He wrote from the province of Voronezh, where he'd been sent to procure horses, but the letter did not ease the countess. Knowing one son was out of danger only made her more anxious about Petya.

Although by the twentieth of August nearly all the Rostovs' acquaintances had left Moscow, and everyone urged the countess to leave as quickly as possible, she refused to hear of going before her treasure — her adored Petya — returned. On August 28 he arrived. The passionate tenderness with which his mother received him displeased the sixteen-year-old officer. Though she hid from him her plan to keep him close, Petya guessed her intentions and, instinctively fearing that he might give in to emotion with her — might "go soft," as he put it to himself — he treated her coolly, avoided her, and during his stay in Moscow attached himself exclusively to Natasha, for whom he had always had an especially brotherly, almost lover-like tenderness.

Due to the count's habitual carelessness, nothing was ready for departure by August 28, and the carts that were supposed to come from their Ryazan and Moscow estates to carry away their belongings didn't arrive until the thirtieth.

From the twenty-eighth to the thirty-first, all Moscow was in an uproar. Every day thousands of men wounded at Borodino were brought in through the Dorogomilov gate and taken to various parts of the city, and thousands of carts carried residents and their possessions out through the other gates. Despite Rostopchin's broadsheets — or because of them, or independently of them — the wildest and most contradictory rumors circulated. Some said no one would be allowed to leave; others said all the icons had been removed from the churches and everyone would be ordered to go. Some claimed another battle after Borodino had routed the French, while others insisted the Russian army had been destroyed. Some talked about the Moscow militia marching to the Three Hills led by the clergy; others whispered that Father Augustin had been forbidden to leave, that traitors had been caught, that peasants were rioting and robbing people on the roads out of Moscow, and so on. But all this was only talk; in reality — though the Council of Fili, at which it was decided to abandon Moscow, had not yet been held — both those who left and those who stayed felt, though they didn't show it, that Moscow would certainly be given up and that they should get away as quickly as possible. Everyone sensed that everything would suddenly collapse and change, but through September 1 nothing had. Like a condemned man being led to execution who looks around and straightens the crooked cap on his head, Moscow involuntarily continued its usual life, though it knew the time of its destruction was near — when the conditions its people were accustomed to would be completely overturned.

During the three days before the occupation, the entire Rostov family was absorbed in various activities. The head of the family, Count Ilya Rostov, drove about the city constantly, collecting rumors from all sides and issuing hasty, confused orders at home about preparations for departure.

The countess watched the packing, was dissatisfied with everything, was constantly chasing after Petya — who kept running away from her — and was jealous of Natasha, with whom he spent all his time. Sonya alone handled the practical side, getting things packed. But lately Sonya had been particularly sad and quiet. Nicholas's letter, in which he mentioned Princess Mary, had prompted joyful comments from the countess — made in Sonya's presence — about seeing Providence at work in bringing the princess and Nicholas together.

"I was never pleased about Bolkonsky's engagement to Natasha," said the countess, "but I always wanted Nicholas to marry the princess, and had a feeling it would happen. What a good match it would be!"

Sonya felt this was true — that the only way to restore the Rostov family's finances was for Nicholas to marry a wealthy woman, and that the princess was an excellent match. It was very bitter for her. But despite her grief — or perhaps because of it — she took on all the difficult work of organizing the packing and was busy all day long. The count and countess turned to her whenever orders needed giving. Petya and Natasha, by contrast, were generally a nuisance and a hindrance. Nearly all day the house rang with their running feet, their shouts, and their spontaneous laughter. They laughed and were joyful not because there was any reason to be, but because gladness and mirth filled their hearts and so everything that happened gave them cause for laughter. Petya was in high spirits because having left home a boy he had returned — as everyone told him — a fine young man; because he was at home; because he'd left Belaya Tserkov where there was no hope of seeing battle anytime soon and had come to Moscow where there would be fighting any day; and chiefly because Natasha, whose lead he always followed, was in high spirits. Natasha was gay because she had been sad too long and now nothing reminded her of the cause of her sadness, and because she was feeling well. She was also happy because she had someone to adore her — the adoration of others was the lubricant her machinery needed to run smoothly, and Petya adored her. Above all, they were gay because there was a war near Moscow, there would be fighting at the city gates, weapons were being handed out, everyone was escaping and going somewhere, and in general something extraordinary was happening — and that is always exciting, especially to the young.
